This tutorial has no slides. It covers the book chapter Surgical Weight Management, written out below from Aldughaither's summary of the same chapter (the full summary is in grey at the end). Facts that appeared in past exams are in red; the questions themselves are on the Obesity lecture.

The obesity epidemic

  • Obesity = excessive accumulation of body fat, assessed by BMI (kg/m²): 18.5–24.9 normal · 25–29.9 overweight · 30–34.9 class I · 35–39.9 class II · ≥ 40 class III (morbid).
  • BMI = weight (kg) / height² (m²).
  • BMI ignores fat distribution — visceral (abdominal) obesity carries more metabolic risk than peripheral fat.
  • US (CDC 2016): 39.8% of adults and 18.5% of youth obese; highest in adults 40–59 (42.8%) and adolescents 12–19 (20.6%); highest in Hispanic (47%) and non-Hispanic Black (46.8%), lowest in non-Hispanic Asian (12.7%); women > men.
  • Health impact: ↑ all-cause mortality; BMI ≥ 40 → up to 8 years shorter life; metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, cancers (breast, colorectal, endometrial), osteoarthritis.
  • Aetiology: caloric excess (calorie-dense, processed food, sugary drinks), sedentary lifestyle, genetic/epigenetic factors — the "thrifty gene" hypothesis (genes that stored fat in times of scarcity cause obesity in times of plenty).

Non-surgical treatment

  • Diet: the goal is caloric reduction — total calorie restriction matters more than macronutrient composition; intensive programmes give ~4–5 kg; regain is common when support stops.
  • Exercise: ≥ 150 min/week moderate aerobic activity; potentiates diet.
  • Psychological: CBT most used; modest alone, useful in a multimodal approach.
  • Drugs — indications: BMI > 30, or > 27 with comorbidities, or inadequate loss/regain after lifestyle change or surgery; stop if no significant loss after 3 months.

Bariatric operations

Restrictive

  • Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG): most performed today; removes 75–80% of the stomach; restrictive + ↓ ghrelin; simpler, no intestinal rerouting; irreversible, possible long-term reflux.
  • Adjustable gastric band (LAGB): silicone band → 30-mL pouch, adjusted via a saline port; least invasive, reversible; high failure rate, slippage, poor long-term results.
  • Vertical banded gastroplasty — obsolete (reflux, stricture, band erosion).

Malabsorptive & mixed

  • Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB): gold standard; 20–30 mL pouch; restrictive + malabsorptive + hormonal changes that improve diabetes; alimentary limb 100–150 cm, biliopancreatic limb 30–60 cm, common channel; better long-term weight loss; deficiencies, dumping, more complex.
  • BPD/duodenal switch: most malabsorptive (sleeve + long bypass); highest weight loss and diabetes resolution; severe malnutrition.
  • SADI: sleeve + single duodeno-ileal anastomosis — simpler BPD/DS; still investigational.
  • Jejunoileal bypass (historical): bypassed 90–95% of the small bowel → malnutrition, diarrhoea, liver failure.

  • Choosing: BMI > 50 → RYGB, BPD/DS or SADI · diabetes/metabolic syndrome → RYGB or BPD/DS · simple/low-risk → LSG or LAGB.
  • Diabetes is the comorbidity that points to RYGB; GERD/oesophagitis → RYGB rather than sleeve.

Outcomes & complications

  • Surgery is the most effective and sustained weight-loss treatment. Measures: %EWL, %TBWL, change in BMI. Weight regain (≥ 20% of maximum loss) in 15–20%.
  • Mortality < 0.3% (LSG 0.1%, RYGB 0.2%); causes of death: sepsis 33%, cardiac 28%, PE 17%.

  • Rapid weight loss → gallstones.

Nutrition after surgery

  • Lifelong iron, B12, calcium, vitamin D; high protein; follow-up every 3–6 months for 2 years.
  • Book diet: liquids 2 weeks → pureed 2–4 weeks → soft 4–6 weeks → regular after 6 weeks; avoid fizzy drinks, high-fat food, alcohol (the doctor's faster weekly plan is on the Obesity page).

Indications — old and new criteria

  • NIH 1991: BMI ≥ 40, or 35–40 + comorbidity (severe OSA, Pickwickian syndrome, cardiovascular disease, severe T2DM, lifestyle limitation), and a realistic understanding of post-op life. Outdated — ignores lower-BMI patients with metabolic disease.
  • ASMBS / Diabetes Surgery Summit (2012): consider surgery at BMI 30–35 with metabolic comorbidity after failed non-surgical treatment.
  • T2DM: BMI ≥ 40 — strongly recommended; 35–40 — poor control despite medication; 30–35 — consider if uncontrolled despite optimal therapy.
  • Asian patients: lower the BMI cut-offs by 2.7 kg/m² (more visceral fat at lower BMI).

Surgical Weight Management

The Obesity Epidemic: Etiology and Impact

Obesity is broadly defined as an excessive accumulation of body fat and is commonly assessed using Body Mass Index (BMI):

BMI (kg/m²)Classification
18.5 - 24.9Normal weight
25 - 29.9Overweight
30 - 34.9Class I Obesity
35 - 39.9Class II Obesity
≥ 40Class III (Morbid) Obesity

While BMI provides a general measure, it does not account for body fat distribution, which is crucial in assessing metabolic risk. Visceral (abdominal) obesity is more strongly associated with metabolic disorders compared to peripheral fat.

Epidemiology
  • The prevalence of obesity in the United States has doubled between 1970 and 2005.
  • According to the CDC (2016):
  • 39.8% of adults and 18.5% of youth (2-19 years) are obese.
  • Adults aged 40-59 have the highest obesity rate (42.8%).
  • Adolescents (12-19 years) have the highest youth obesity rate (20.6%).
  • Obesity rates vary across ethnicities, with Hispanic (47%) and Non- Hispanic Black Americans (46.8%) having the highest rates, while Non-Hispanic Asians (12.7%) have the lowest.
  • Women have higher obesity rates than men across all ethnic groups.
Health Impact of Obesity

Obesity is associated with a significant increase in all-cause mortality and a reduction in life expectancy. Individuals with a BMI ≥40 may experience up to an 8-year reduction in lifespan. The condition increases the risk of:

  • Metabolic Syndrome: A cluster of conditions including abdominal obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hypertension.
  • Cardiovascular Diseases: Increased risk of heart disease, stroke, and hypertension.
  • Type 2 Diabetes: Strongly linked to obesity due to insulin resistance.
  • Cancer: Elevated risk for cancers such as breast, colorectal, and endometrial cancer.
  • Musculoskeletal Disorders: Increased incidence of osteoarthritis due to excess weight.
Etiology of Obesity

The rapid rise in obesity is attributed to multiple genetic, environmental, and behavioral factors:

1. Caloric Excess & Dietary Changes
  • Increased availability of calorie-dense, nutrient-poor foods.
  • High consumption of processed foods, sugary beverages, and refined carbohydrates.
2. Sedentary Lifestyle
  • Declining daily physical activity due to urbanization and technology.
  • Inverse relationship between physical activity and obesity.
3. Genetic & Epigenetic Factors
  • Obesity has a heritable component, with certain genetic variations favoring energy storage and fat accumulation.
  • The "Thrifty Gene Hypothesis" suggests that genetic adaptations favoring fat storage for survival in times of food scarcity contribute to obesity in modern times of abundance.
Nonsurgical Treatment Options for Obesity: Behavioral and Medical
Behavioral Modifications

Behavioral strategies for obesity management primarily include dietary modifications, physical activity, and psychological interventions. These approaches aim to achieve long-term, sustainable weight loss.

Dietary Modification
  • The primary goal of dietary modification is to achieve caloric reduction.
  • Various dietary programs exist, including low-carbohydrate, low-fat, and Mediterranean diets.
  • Research indicates that total calorie restriction rather than macronutrient composition is the primary factor in weight loss.
  • Intensive dietary interventions can result in an average weight loss of 4-5 kg.
  • Long-term adherence is necessary, as weight regain is common once support is withdrawn.
Physical Activity
  • Regular physical activity increases caloric expenditure and enhances metabolic health.
  • Guidelines recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise per week.
  • High-intensity exercises may be more effective for weight loss but may not be suitable for patients with cardiovascular or musculoskeletal comorbidities.
  • When combined with dietary modification, exercise potentiates weight loss and improves cardiovascular health.
Psychological Interventions
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is the most used psychological intervention.
  • Group therapy and counseling can improve motivation and compliance with weight loss regimens.
  • Alone, psychological interventions result in only modest weight loss but are beneficial when incorporated into a multimodal approach.
Pharmacologic Interventions

Pharmacotherapy serves as an adjunct to behavioral modifications, aiding in appetite suppression and metabolic enhancement.

Indications for Pharmacotherapy
  • Patients with BMI > 30, or BMI > 27 with obesity-related comorbidities.
  • Patients experiencing inadequate weight loss or weight regain after lifestyle modifications or bariatric surgery.
  • If no significant weight loss occurs after 3 months, the medication should be discontinued.
FDA-Approved Weight Loss Medications
1. Phentermine
  • Mechanism: Sympathomimetic amine that increases norepinephrine and dopamine release.
  • Efficacy: 5-6% total body weight loss (TBWL).
  • Approved for short-term use (up to 3 months).
  • Side Effects: Increased heart rate, hypertension, dry mouth, insomnia.
2. Orlistat (Xenical, Alli)
  • Mechanism: Inhibits pancreatic and gastric lipase, reducing fat absorption.
  • Efficacy: 5-10% TBWL.
  • Side Effects: Gastrointestinal discomfort, diarrhea, fecal incontinence, flatulence.
3. Phentermine/Topiramate (Qsymia)
  • Mechanism: Combination of phentermine (appetite suppressant) and topiramate (GABA receptor agonist).
  • Efficacy: 7-10% TBWL.
  • Side Effects: Headache, paresthesia, dry mouth.
4. Bupropion/Naltrexone (Contrave)
  • Mechanism: Enhances hypothalamic release of alpha-melanocyte- stimulating hormone, leading to appetite suppression.
  • Efficacy: 5-6% TBWL.
  • Side Effects: Headache, insomnia, tremors, constipation.
5. Lorcaserin (Belviq)
  • Mechanism: Serotonin (5-HT2C) receptor agonist, reducing appetite via the hypothalamic proopiomelanocortin pathway.
  • Efficacy: 5-7% TBWL.
  • Side Effects: Hallucinations, headache, potential cardiovascular risks.
6. Liraglutide (Saxenda)
  • Mechanism: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, promoting satiety and insulin sensitivity.
  • Efficacy: 7-9% TBWL.
  • Side Effects: Nausea, diarrhea, rare cases of pancreatitis.
Surgical Options for Obesity
1. Types of Bariatric Surgeries
A. Restrictive Procedures

These limit the volume of food intake by creating a smaller stomach reservoir.

  • Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy (LSG)
  • Most performed procedure today.
  • Involves the removal of 75-80% of the stomach, leaving a narrow gastric tube.
  • Effects: Restrictive, reduces ghrelin levels (hunger hormone), leading to metabolic benefits.
  • Advantages: Simpler, lower complication rates, and no intestinal rerouting.
  • Disadvantages: Irreversible; possible long-term reflux.
  • Laparoscopic Adjustable Gastric Banding (LAGB)
  • Silicone band placed around the stomach to create a 30-mL pouch.
  • Adjustable by inflating/deflating a saline-filled balloon in the band.
  • Advantages: Least invasive, reversible, no malabsorption.
  • Disadvantages: High failure rate, risk of band slippage, poor long- term weight loss outcomes.
  • Vertical Banded Gastroplasty (VBG) (Obsolete)
  • Stomach is stapled vertically, leaving a small passage with a prosthetic band.
  • Failed due to: Severe reflux, nausea, stricture formation, and band erosion.
B. Malabsorptive & Mixed Procedures

These alter digestion by reducing nutrient absorption and food intake.

  • Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB)
  • Considered the gold standard for weight loss surgery.
  • Procedure: Creates a 20-30 mL stomach pouch, bypassing part of the small intestine.
  • Effects: Restrictive & malabsorptive, hormonal changes improve diabetes.
  • Key Components:
    • Alimentary limb (100-150 cm): Carries food without bile/pancreatic enzymes.
    • Biliopancreatic limb (30-60 cm): Carries digestive enzymes.
    • Common channel: Where food meets enzymes for digestion.
  • Advantages: Superior long-term weight loss, effective in diabetes.
  • Disadvantages: Nutrient deficiencies, dumping syndrome, more complex surgery.
  • Biliopancreatic Diversion with Duodenal Switch (BPD/DS)
  • Most malabsorptive procedure, combines a sleeve gastrectomy with rerouting of the intestine.
  • Procedure: Removes most of the stomach, bypasses significant intestine length.
  • Effects: Major weight loss & metabolic benefits but higher risk of malnutrition.
  • Advantages: Highest weight loss & diabetes resolution.
  • Disadvantages: Severe malnutrition, long-term vitamin supplementation required.
  • Single-Anastomosis Duodeno-Ileal Bypass (SADI)
  • Simplified version of BPD/DS to reduce complications.
  • Procedure: Sleeve gastrectomy + single anastomosis to the ileum.
  • Effects: Similar weight loss benefits but less severe malabsorption.
  • Advantages: Easier surgery, fewer complications than BPD/DS.
  • Disadvantages: Still investigational, long-term outcomes unclear.
C. Historical Procedures (No Longer Used)
  • Jejunoileal Bypass (JIB)
  • Early malabsorptive procedure bypassing 90-95% of the small intestine.
  • Discontinued due to: Severe malnutrition, diarrhea, dehydration, and liver failure.

3. Choosing the Right Procedure
  • For patients with severe obesity (BMI >50): RYGB, BPD/DS, or SADI.
  • For patients with diabetes/metabolic syndrome: RYGB or BPD/DS.
  • For patients wanting a simple procedure with fewer risks: LSG or LAGB.
  • For those concerned about long-term malnutrition: LSG or LAGB preferred.
4. Long-Term Considerations
  • Nutritional Deficiencies:
  • RYGB & BPD/DS require lifelong vitamin supplementation (B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D).
  • LSG has fewer deficiencies but may still require supplements.
  • Weight Regain Risks:
  • LAGB and VBG have the highest failure rates.
  • LSG & RYGB show sustained long-term success but require lifestyle changes.
  • Dumping Syndrome (RYGB, BPD/DS):
  • Rapid gastric emptying leading to nausea, diarrhea, and sweating after meals.
Efficacy, Complications, and Outcomes of Bariatric Surgery
1. Efficacy of Bariatric Surgery

Bariatric surgery is the most effective and sustained weight loss intervention, outperforming behavioral and pharmacologic therapies. Weight loss is commonly measured by:

  • Excess Weight Loss (EWL) (percentage of weight lost beyond ideal body weight).
  • Total Body Weight Loss (TBWL) (percentage of total body weight lost).
  • Change in BMI (absolute or percentage decrease).

B. Long-Term Outcomes
  • Weight regain (≥20% of max weight lost) occurs in 15-20% of patients.
  • RYGB and BPD/DS have the highest long-term success rates.
  • LAGB has the highest failure rate due to inadequate weight loss and band- related complications.
  • LSG has become the most common surgery due to its simplicity and effectiveness.
2. Complications of Bariatric Surgery

Bariatric surgery is generally safe, with mortality rates <0.3%, but complications can occur.

  • Dumping Syndrome (common in RYGB & BPD/DS)
  • Symptoms: Nausea, diarrhea, sweating, dizziness after eating.
  • Management: Avoid high-sugar foods, eat smaller meals.

  • Signs: Vague abdominal pain, intermittent obstruction.
  • Diagnosis: CT scan showing "swirling" of mesenteric vessels.
  • Management: Emergency surgery.
  • Prevention: Routine closure of mesenteric defects during surgery.
3. Safety and Mortality Rates
  • Overall mortality rates:
  • LSG: 0.1%
  • RYGB: 0.2%
  • BPD/DS: Higher due to malnutrition risks.
  • Most common causes of death post-surgery: 1. Sepsis (33%) 2. Cardiac events (28%) 3. Pulmonary embolism (17%)
4. Key Considerations for Patients
A. Who Benefits the Most?
  • BMI >40 kg/m² or BMI >35 kg/m² with comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension).
  • Patients with metabolic syndrome (RYGB & BPD/DS best for diabetes).
  • LSG is a good option for those who want fewer risks and no intestinal rerouting.
B. Who Should Avoid Surgery?
  • Severe heart/lung disease (high surgical risk).
  • Untreated psychiatric illness (binge eating, substance abuse).
  • Noncompliant patients (require lifelong follow-up & dietary changes).
5. Postoperative Nutrition & Lifestyle
  • Vitamin & Mineral Deficiencies (especially in RYGB & BPD/DS)
  • Iron, B12, calcium, vitamin D supplements required lifelong.
  • Protein intake must be high to prevent muscle loss.
  • Routine follow-ups every 3-6 months in the first 2 years.
  • Dietary Recommendations
  • Phase 1: Liquid diet (2 weeks)
  • Phase 2: Pureed foods (2-4 weeks)
  • Phase 3: Soft solids (4-6 weeks)
  • Phase 4: Regular diet (after 6 weeks)
  • Avoid carbonated beverages, high-fat foods, and alcohol.
Nutritional Consequences & Surgical Indications in Bariatric Surgery
1. Nutritional Consequences of Bariatric Surgery

Post-bariatric surgery malnutrition remains a major long-term complication, despite modern techniques minimizing risks. The main causes include:

  • Reduced caloric and nutrient intake due to restricted food consumption.
  • Intestinal bypass altering nutrient absorption (especially in RYGB and BPD/DS).
A. Iron Deficiency
  • Absorption site: Duodenum and proximal jejunum.
  • Causes of deficiency: 1. Reduced gastric acid production (affects iron solubility and uptake). 2. Bypass of iron-absorbing enterocytes in the duodenum. 3. Reduced intake of iron-rich foods (meat, dairy).
  • Prevalence: >10% of patients 5 years post-surgery.
  • Management: Routine iron supplementation is recommended.
B. Vitamin B12 & Folate Deficiency
  • Absorption site: Vitamin B12 absorption mainly in the ileum but requires intrinsic factor from the stomach.
  • Causes of deficiency: 1. Reduced intrinsic factor production after gastric resection. 2. Bypass of the duodenum and proximal jejunum, where B12 binds to intrinsic factor. 3. Reduced dietary intake of B12-rich foods.
  • Prevalence: 20-35% of RYGB & BPD/DS patients experience deficiency at 5 years.
  • Consequences: Macrocytic anemia due to B12 or folate deficiency.
  • Management:
  • Oral supplementation for folate.
  • Intramuscular B12 injections may be required for severe deficiency.
C. Fat-Soluble Vitamin Deficiencies (A, D, E, K)
  • Most common in: BPD/DS due to severe fat malabsorption.
  • Prevalence:
  • Vitamin A deficiency: Up to 65%.
  • Vitamin K deficiency: Up to 60%.
  • Vitamin D deficiency: Up to 70%.
  • Clinical impact: Most patients are asymptomatic, but severe cases may cause vision problems (vitamin A), bleeding disorders (vitamin K), and bone loss (vitamin D).
  • Management: Routine multivitamin supplementation with high-dose vitamin D.
D. Vitamin D, Calcium, and Bone Health
  • Absorption site: Calcium is primarily absorbed in the duodenum & proximal jejunum.
  • Causes of deficiency:
  • Bypass of calcium absorption sites.
  • Fat malabsorption reduces vitamin D levels, affecting calcium uptake.
  • Prevalence: 10% of post-surgical patients develop calcium deficiency.
  • Consequences:
  • Decreased Bone Mineral Density (BMD) in 8-13% of patients.
  • Increased risk of fractures (2x higher than general population).
  • Management:
  • Lifelong calcium & vitamin D supplements.
  • Regular monitoring of calcium, vitamin D, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels.
2. Expanding Surgical Indications & Patient Selection

Proper patient selection is critical for maximizing benefits and minimizing risks in bariatric surgery.

A. Standard NIH Criteria (1991)

According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Consensus on Gastrointestinal Surgery for Severe Obesity, bariatric surgery is indicated for:

1. BMI ≥ 40 kg/m² (Severe obesity).

2. BMI 35-40 kg/m² + obesity-related comorbidities, such as:

  • Severe sleep apnea.
  • Pickwickian syndrome (obesity hypoventilation syndrome).
  • Cardiovascular diseases.
  • Severe type 2 diabetes.
  • Significant lifestyle hindrance due to obesity.

3. Patient must have a clear and realistic understanding of post-surgical life

  • changes.
B. Issues with NIH Criteria
  • Outdated (based on 1991 data).
  • Does not account for improvements in surgical techniques.
  • Fails to include lower BMI patients with severe metabolic disease.
C. Newer Recommendations: ASMBS & Diabetes Surgery Summit (DSS-D)

In 2012, the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (ASMBS) and Second Diabetes Surgery Summit (DSS-D) proposed updated guidelines:

1. Lower BMI Threshold for Surgery
  • Bariatric surgery should be considered for BMI 30-35 kg/m² patients with:
  • Metabolic comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension).
  • Failed non-surgical interventions (diet, medications).
2. Specific Recommendations for Type 2 Diabetes
  • Class III obesity (BMI ≥ 40): Surgery is strongly recommended for diabetes.
  • Class II obesity (BMI 35-40): Surgery is recommended for poor glycemic control despite medications.
  • Class I obesity (BMI 30-35): Surgery should be considered if diabetes is uncontrolled despite optimal therapy.
3. Adjusted BMI Criteria for Asian Patients
  • BMI cutoffs should be lowered by 2.7 kg/m² for Asian populations.
  • Reason: Asians have higher visceral fat and greater metabolic risk at lower BMI levels.
